newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Markets too gloomy on Pakistan economy - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Markets too gloomy on Pakistan economy - analyst.

text.p: Perceptions of a looming economic crisis in Pakistan are overblown and markets are overreacting, a prominent stocks analyst said on Wednesday.

"We are not denying that the economy has certain problems, but the situation is not as bad as the media and the markets perceive," Kalim Aziz, senior analyst and head of research at ING Baring Securities, told Reuters.

Brokers and bankers say stock prices may slide and foreign lenders may reduce their exposure to Pakistan after indications last week that the International Monetary Fund have refused to reactivate stalled tranches of a $600 million standby loan.
"There is a need for structural reforms and instituting these reforms means swallowing bitter pills, but we simply state that the economy is in transition," Aziz said.
The Karachi 100-share index sagged 10.82 points, or 0.79 percent, to 1,354.26 at noon on Wednesday as blue chips tumbled.

Dealers said they expected sentiment to remain negative on perceptions of a bleak economic outlook. "Sentiment is bearish. Political trouble and bad economic prospects have jolted investors' confidence," one dealer said.
Aziz said an IMF refusal to release tranches of the standby loan would not necessarily cause a balance of payments crisis.

Aziz said there was no risk of default on Pakistan's foreign debt now or in the near future, saying forthcoming payments estimated at $500 million to $550 million must have been taken into account in the fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) budget.
He said expectations that the IMF would release stalled tranches of the $600 million standby loan were unrealistic.

The government said last week that three days of talks with the International Monetary Fund in Washington had produced an "understanding" on the main elements of economic stabilisation and structural reforms, but did not mention the standby loan.
IMF officials say they must complete a long-delayed review of Pakistan's economic performance before making any new disbursements, but have set no date for sending a mission.
"It is a very good sign that the IMF is looking to the government for a complete and implementable structural reform proposal before any release of funds," Aziz said.
He said he had advised investors to take a wait-and-see attitude this month, but they should find good value next month.
"It may come as a surprise, but the government of Pakistan has an untapped source of about $6 billion of forex reserves committed by large donors and international lending agencies," he said.
"You cannot expect the IMF to release the tranches on the back of a visit by government officials," he said.
